extracted.intended_audience: Patent attorneys, litigators, and in-house counsel handling US Section 101 eligibility and related litigation/prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting US patent applications and infringement complaints to survive Section 101 challenges and early motions to dismiss. Focuses on pleadings, specifications, claim-construction strategy, disclosures, and citing authorities to show inventive concepts over prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain benefits of the invention over the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly illustrate the benefits of the claimed technology compared to the prior art in patent applications and specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit found that explaining the benefits of the invention helps get past motions to dismiss even if it may not ensure Section 101 validity. Judges look to the specification for information showing why patents are different from the prior art; there is a 'heightened standard' in practice. Drafting applications to explain advantages and improvements is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the specification to show how the patent differs from prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Address in the specification the ways the invention differs from and improves on prior art technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although it is acceptable to file without addressing every difference, companies will benefit from addressing these questions in their applications because courts often look to the specification when assessing eligibility and inventive concept allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plead plausible, factual allegations of inventive concepts in complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Include plausible and factual allegations in complaints that the claims recite inventive concepts or improvements over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit reversed a dismissal because the complaint contained plausible factual allegations that claims included inventive concepts. Well-pleaded allegations of an inventive concept can be enough to survive a motion to dismiss under Section 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft clearer complaints with updated citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Make complaints clearer, specific, and supported with appropriate citations and authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigators should generally make complaints clearer in light of this ruling and consider adding new citations to support allegations. Clearer pleadings can improve chances of surviving early dispositive motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and take claim-construction positions early
rubrics_metrics.description: Address claim-construction issues and, where appropriate, state claim-construction positions early in litigation and in briefing to avoid adverse rulings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court had not conducted claim construction but the Federal Circuit adopted the plaintiff’s construction and reversed. Plaintiffs often avoid early positions, but taking positions earlier can help overcome motions to dismiss; courts typically set timelines for exchanging proposed constructions, but earlier consideration may be advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and rebut defendants' Section 101 arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Proactively anticipate common defendant arguments (e.g., that innovations are not inventive because only standard computer elements are claimed) and rebut them in pleadings and briefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel can cite this case to counter claims that purported inventions lack inventiveness because they use standard computing equipment. Anticipatory arguments and tailored explanations of improvements can blunt such defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose material information (duty of candour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain the duty of candour by disclosing material information in prosecution and related filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants have a duty to disclose material information. While the duty is longstanding, Section 101 case law means judges often want to know why patents are different from prior art, increasing the practical importance of candid, informative disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize practical, useful improvements (especially for computer/network inventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame claimed subject matter as providing useful, practical improvements (for example, to computer networks), which can be patentable even if standard components are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court stated that useful improvements to computer networks were patentable regardless of whether the network comprised standard computing equipment. Emphasizing practical technical improvements helps counter arguments that claims are only abstract or noninventive.
